dimensions.note: secretAccessKey is .meta({ sensitive: true }); accessKeyId deliberately is not, matching the published @sntxrr/restic and b2 extensions where the key ID is an identifier and the secret half is separate. The linter flags this as medium — it is a reasoned, consistent convention, not an oversight. Defence is layered: runRclone refuses to spawn if either credential appears in argv on EITHER host (ps is world-readable on both); credentials travel as a docker --env-file streamed down the SSH stdin pipe into a FIFO in a private 0700 dir, so they reach neither argv nor the NAS filesystem; stderr is redacted at the subprocess boundary because rclone echoes remote config into error text; and a credential containing a newline is rejected rather than silently truncated by --env-file, since a truncated key fails as an auth error and reads like the wrong key rather than a corrupted one.

Five call sites. Each rung's real output is the resource it writes; logs carry what an operator needs to act — an unreachable share with its classified reason, per-pack failures naming the pack and classification, and completion facts. Failure detail is captured on the resource (truncated, redacted) rather than only in a log line that may not be retained.

rclone's exit codes are encoded and classified rather than collapsed to pass/fail, and inconclusive (5 temporary, 8 transfer-limit, 10 duration-limit, plus timeout) is kept distinct from failure so a capped or retried run is not recorded as a broken archive. --error-on-no-transfer makes code 9 a distinct 'nothing to transfer' outcome instead of an ambiguous 0. Verified live: a transport failure returning docker's 125 classified as exit-125 and was reported as an unreachable share with the detail preserved, rather than throwing.

99 tests, confirmed by exit status; the writeResource stub parses against the REAL spec schemas; a fake ssh drives the true subprocess boundary; two tests execute the generated remote shell for real. Rungs 1-4 are verified live (37 objects / 200,840,300 B as DEEP_ARCHIVE, verify zero-delta), and restoreRequest is now verified live in three states: an accepted request, an idempotent re-request of an in-flight retrieval, and a path matching no object. THE REMAINING GAP: restoreDrill has not completed against real Deep Archive — a Standard-tier retrieval is in flight and the drill cannot run until it materialises. Recovery is therefore still unproven end to end, and by this suite's own rule an archive that has never been restored is an assumption. Three live bugs so far (DSM refusing to open /dev/stdin, GLACIER_DEEP_ARCHIVE not being a storage class, and restore pointing at a file instead of a directory) were each invisible to a fully green suite, which is why this dimension stays ISSUE until the drill passes.

copy, never sync: nine destructive subcommands refused at the runner, each asserted. --immutable by default. --no-traverse coupled to --max-age in code so the cost trap cannot be split. restoreRequest is idempotent by design — S3 answers a re-request for an in-flight retrieval with 409 RestoreAlreadyInProgress, which is recognised and recorded as success rather than as a failure, because re-running while waiting is the obvious operator move. Restore filters are anchored and glob-escaped so a re-run cannot widen its own blast radius.

Exit codes and billing rules are encoded from observed behaviour, not docs. Storage classes are validated against the set S3 accepts before being judged on cost, after a live 400 InvalidStorageClass. Most importantly, `backend restore` is now known NOT to signal per-object outcomes through its exit code: a per-object S3 error exits 0 with the failure only in the JSON Status, and a filter matching nothing also exits 0. Both are parsed and both are treated as failures, because trusting the exit code turns a mis-typed path into a drill that quietly cannot pass. ETags remain unused for verification, since a multipart ETag is not a content MD5.

The remote temp dir is removed by a trap on EXIT INT TERM; the FIFO writer is killed rather than waited on, because if docker dies before opening the FIFO the writer is still blocked in open() and a wait would hang until the six-hour timeout. Both paths are asserted, and the no-hang case is executed. Subprocesses run under an AbortController with a six-hour default. Incomplete multipart uploads are handled where they must be — a bucket lifecycle rule, documented in SETUP — because orphaned parts are billed and invisible to ListObjects; a live run left zero.

The shipped surface is rclone_archive.ts, README.md, LICENSE.md and manifest.yaml. Audited against every real identifier extracted from live output — hostnames, domain, tailnet IPs, AWS account id, bucket name, share names, archived content names, access keys: none appear. The only concrete paths are the generic /volume1/homes and one comment naming a share used deliberately as a real-path test fixture per CONVENTIONS. Repo history was also swept; no credential reaches it.

zod v4 throughout, for global arguments and all four resource specs. A test asserts every spec has a schema and that methods write only declared specs, and because the test context parses through the real schema, a drifting resource shape fails the suite rather than reaching the datastore.

All four specs are lifetime infinite with garbageCollection 50. Infinite is deliberate for an archive of last resort: the inventory, transfer, verification and retrieval records ARE the audit trail, and the churn calculation reads the previous scan, so expiring history would silently disable cost and churn detection.

Deliberately not a CRUD model. This is a cost-ordered verification ladder over a destination it must never mutate destructively; there is no create/update/delete surface by design, and the runner refuses the nine rclone subcommands that remove data. The bucket and IAM key are consumed, not created — the suite's blast radius stops at 'uploads to the wrong prefix'.

Three checks. source-path-absolute exists because a relative path does not fail — docker silently creates a named volume and the archive would be of nothing. credentials-present catches an unresolved vault reference. archive-storage-class now asks two ordered questions, validity then cost, because reporting an invalid class as 'not an archive tier' sends you looking at cost instead of spelling. The absence of a restore-acknowledgement check is deliberate and documented in place: checks receive only globalArgs, so it would reject --input allowRestore=true before execute ran.
Each spec writes a distinct instance name derived from shareName, and a test asserts the names are distinct across specs so one rung cannot overwrite another's record.

Churn wiring is documented to use data.latest(<model>, <RESOURCE INSTANCE>), with an explicit warning that the second argument is the share name and not the spec name — passing the spec name fails at expression resolution, which is a confusing failure worth pre-empting in the schema description.
First publish; no previously published version exists, so no upgrade entries apply. The registry confirmed no version drift to check against.
